title: Microburst spectator runlog - notes and quick findings
content:
Purpose:
Quick exploratory run to reproduce intermittent p99 spikes when a small subset of tenants ("spectators") suddenly send short, high-rate requests (10–50ms payloads). Goal: capture time-aligned telemetry, kv-cache behavior, and scheduler/batcher response; produce actionable next steps.

Hypothesis:
- Spikes are caused by thin, high-QPS bursts that escape batching windows and thrash the GPU hotpool and KV cache priming.
- Spectator pattern (small % of clients hitting same shard) amplifies cold-path serialization and queue head-of-line blocking.

Testbed (local-ish staging):
- 6-node serving fleet, heterogeneous GPUs (2x A10, 4x T4 emulated), model: gpt-smallish-6B (int8), tokenizer: huggingface-encoder v1.2
- Runtime: rwinference-v0.63 (local build), batching config: max_batch_tokens=4096, batch_timeout_ms=6, max_batch_size=64
- KV cache: LRU per-instance, capacity 2M tokens, prefix caching enabled for warm requests
- Load generator: custom locust script + spectator shim that pins 5% of virtual users to shard-2

Workload pattern used:
- Background steady traffic: 120 rps total, 80% short (40–60 tokens), 20% long (200–600 tokens)
- Spectator injection: at t=60s, 5% of clients start 200 qps bursts lasting 6s each, repeated every 30s for 10 minutes

Commands (how to reproduce quickly):
- start load: ./scripts/run_spectator.sh --duration 600 --bg-rps 120 --spectator-qps 200 --burst-dur 6
- collect traces: curl http://obs-agent/flush && aws s3 cp /tmp/microburst-20250917/ s3://perf-logs/microburst/2025-09-17/ --recursive

Run timeline & notable telemetry (timestamps relative to run start):
- 00:00–00:55: baseline stable, p50=18ms, p95=42ms, p99=78ms, overall qps ~120
- 01:00: first spectator burst (6s): p50=22ms, p95=110ms, p99=420ms -> backend hotpath CPU queues increased, one instance reported 2x syscall wait
- 01:36: second burst: p99 peaked at 390ms, but one T4 instance saw sustained CPU load and queue length climbed from 3->16 requests
- 02:30–04:00: repeated bursts, observed gradual KV cache hit-rate drop on shard-2 from 87% -> 61% (prefill not keeping up)
- 05:10: recovery period: batcher increased frequency of tiny batches (timeout firing) causing more small-device kernel launches, leading to GPU utilization jitter

Key metrics (aggregated, sample window 01:00-05:00):
- baseline p99 (no bursts): 78ms
- during bursts p99 median: 385ms (stdev 45ms)
- observed small-batch rate (batches < 4 requests): 8% -> 32% during burst windows
- KV cache hit-rate (shard-2): 87% -> 61% during run
- GPU kernel launch rate: +3.7x during bursts

Quick ASCII timeline (p99 in ms by 30s buckets):
[0 ]  50 |====
[30]  60 |=====
[60] 420 |==================== (burst start)
[90] 380 |=================  (burst)
[120]110 |======
[150] 95 |====
[180]350 |===============
...

Observations / raw notes:
- Spectator bursts consistently localized to shard-2 (we pinned them). That instance showed cache churn and more frequent small batches.
- Small batches correlate strongly with p99 spikes. Timeout=6ms might be too aggressive for mixed workloads with microbursts.
- KV-prefill doesn't keep up when many new short contexts arrive; we see prefill QPS exceed prefill-handler capacity and requests fall back to cold path.
- T4 nodes are more sensitive; A10s handle bursts better (lower p99 under same load). Could be kernel warmup/geometric throughput differences.
- Some request traces show head-of-line blocking: long requests in the same batch delaying short ones for extra 10–60ms. Dynamic priority lanes might help.

Immediate quick mitigations attempted (manual toggles during run):
- raised batch_timeout_ms -> 10ms: reduced small-batch fraction from 32%->18% but increased p50 by ~6ms; p99 still improved (~250ms peak)
- enabled aggressive KV-prefetching for known-short clients: cache hit-rate recovered to ~78% but CPU prefill QPS spiked (extra CPU cost)
- isolated spectator clients onto separate serving pool: p99 for main pool returned to baseline but spectator pool saturated and showed worse p99 (tradeoff)

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the optimal batch_timeout that balances p50 vs p99 for mixed short/long traffic under microburst patterns? Run a sweep: [2,4,6,8,12,20] ms with same burst profile.
- Can we throttle prefill consumers or apply a token-bucket to prefill pipeline to avoid CPU overload?
- Need to reproduce with homogenous A10 fleet to confirm device sensitivity.
- Instrument kernel launch latency per-GPU to see if there is a critical threshold where launching dominates.
- Consider implementing a short-request fastpath (preliminary design in INF-4823).

Next steps (concrete):
- (Today) schedule timeout sweep (2–20ms) across 3 repeated runs, capture full traces + batch composition. Owner: Isha
- (This week) run homogenous A10 test and T4-only test, compare p50/p95/p99. Owner: Liam
- (Next week) prototype short-request fastpath in a branch (PR link in linked_artifacts). Owner: Zara

Notes-to-self:
- Make sure to include per-batch contexts count in telemetry (not just token counts).
- Add a small synthetic test that warms KV cache for spectator identities before injecting bursts (to separate cache priming vs batching effect).
- Remind infra to keep staging GPU drivers consistent with prod (we saw a driver minor mismatch).

Appendix (snippets):
- locust snippet (spectator pin):
    class SpectatorBehaviour(HttpUser):
        def on_start(self):
            if self.environment.runner.user_count * 0.05 < 1: return
        @task
        def short_req(self):
            client.post('/v1/generate', json={ 'input': 'hi' })

- quick grep to find small batches in traces: grep '\"batch_size\"' -n perf-traces | jq 'select(.batch_size < 4)' | wc -l

End — raw scratch. Keep this around until sweep done.
